name: The Noble Lie
statement: Plato imagined rulers spreading a useful myth to bind citizens together and reconcile them to their place.
statementAccent: a useful myth to bind citizens together
meaning: The noble lie is a concept from Plato's Republic, in Book III, where Socrates proposes a gennaion pseudos, variously translated as a noble lie, noble falsehood, or magnificent myth, meaning a untruth knowingly propagated by a ruling elite in order to promote social harmony and preserve the order of the ideal city. The specific noble lie Plato proposes is the myth of the metals. Citizens are to be told, first, that they were all born from the earth itself, making them brothers of one soil and bound to their city, and second, that the god who fashioned them mixed different metals into their souls: gold in the rulers or guardians, silver in the auxiliaries or soldiers, and bronze and iron in the farmers and craftsmen. This myth is meant to justify the class structure of the just city, foster unity and loyalty, and reconcile each citizen to their social role and the division of labor. The noble lie has become one of the most discussed and controversial ideas in political philosophy, raising the question of whether rulers may rightfully deceive citizens for the common good. It is invoked in debates about propaganda, paternalism, civic myth, and the ethics of political deception, and it has been sharply criticized as a licence for manipulation.
mechanism: The noble lie is a founding myth deliberately instilled in the citizens of Plato's ideal city, Kallipolis, to secure their cohesion and their acceptance of its social order. In Plato's account, the rulers would tell all citizens a story with two parts. The first is a myth of autochthony: that the citizens were not raised and educated by human parents but were formed within the earth, their true mother, and only later emerged, so that they should regard the land as their mother to defend and one another as earth-born brothers, cultivating patriotism and solidarity. The second is the myth of the metals: that the god who created them blended metals into the souls of each, gold for those fit to rule, silver for the warrior-auxiliaries, and bronze and iron for the producers, with the warning that the city will be ruined if a person of baser metal ever rules. Because souls are supposedly stamped with these metals, each citizen has a natural place in the hierarchy of the city, and the myth reconciles them to that place and to the division of labor, while allowing, in principle, for a child to be moved between classes if their metal differs from their parents. The falsehood is called noble because it is told not for the rulers' private advantage but, in Plato's view, for the good of the whole community and its stability.

examples.text: Citizens are told the god mixed gold in the rulers, silver in the soldiers, and bronze and iron in the producers, justifying the classes.
The myth of autochthony has citizens believe they were formed within the earth, their common mother, fostering unity and patriotism.
The falsehood is called noble because it is told for the good and stability of the whole community, not the rulers' private gain.

whyItMatters: The noble lie is one of the most provocative and enduring ideas in political philosophy, because it poses in the sharpest form the question of whether rulers may deceive their citizens for the sake of the common good. By proposing that the guardians of his ideal city instill a founding myth to promote unity and reconcile people to their social roles, Plato raised issues about the relationship between truth, power, and social order that remain urgent, and the noble lie has become a touchstone for debates about propaganda, civic religion, paternalism, myth-making, and the ethics of political deception. It challenges the assumption that a just society must rest on truth, and it forces reflection on whether beneficial falsehoods, or noble lies, could ever be justified, and at what cost to autonomy and trust. The idea has been read in radically different ways, from the sympathetic interpretations of Leo Strauss to the fierce condemnation of Karl Popper, who saw it as a blueprint for totalitarian manipulation, and it continues to shape discussions of political myth and the manipulation of belief.

limits: The noble lie must be presented with care about translation and interpretation, and it is deeply controversial. The Greek gennaion pseudos is not straightforwardly rendered noble lie; some scholars prefer noble falsehood, magnificent myth, or story, arguing that lie is harsher than the Greek implies, so the very label carries an interpretive choice. The passage is Book III of the Republic, commonly cited around Stephanus numbers 414 to 415, and there is genuine scholarly debate over whether Plato meant the proposal seriously or with irony. The idea has been fiercely criticized: Karl Popper, in The Open Society and Its Enemies, attacked the noble lie as a model of authoritarian propaganda locking citizens into a rigid caste system and likened its foundation myth to modern myths of blood and soil.
misreadings: The noble lie is not obviously endorsed by Plato as simply good; whether he meant it seriously or ironically is debated, and critics like Popper condemn it as authoritarian manipulation. The phrase noble lie is a translation choice, since gennaion pseudos may be rendered more mildly as noble falsehood or myth. And it is called noble not because lying is harmless but because it is told for the community's good, a justification many reject, so treating the noble lie as Plato's plain endorsement, as unambiguously a lie, or as clearly benign, misreads a contested and disturbing proposal.
origin: A concept from Plato's Republic, Book III, where Socrates proposes a gennaion pseudos, a noble lie such as the myth of the metals, told by rulers to promote unity and preserve the order of the ideal city.
